885.bp: When heavy rain falls on a city, water pools in low-lying areas and overwhelms drainage systems, flooding streets and damaging homes. To warn residents and dispatch emergency crews in time, we need to predict not just whether it will rain, but where water will actually collect on the ground—which depends on both rainfall and terrain shape, not just weather forecasts.
885.wh: Standard weather models predict rain very well, but they assume flat ground and uniform drainage. Real cities have hills, valleys, pipelines, and compacted soil that route water in hidden ways. Machine learning can spot patterns in historical water depth data, but it treats rainfall and terrain as separate puzzles instead of understanding the actual physics—how water flows downhill and accumulates in valleys—so it misses critical interactions.
The core tension: traditional physics-based models need perfect terrain and weather data that no city has; data-driven models ignore the geography entirely and just match historical noise.
885.ap: Waterlogformer runs two parallel neural pathways. One learns rainfall patterns over time (how rain grows and shrinks hour to hour). The other combines this with static terrain maps to compute where water naturally collects as it flows downhill. A separate fusion module then joins these two insights, using a learning technique that pushes the model to notice which neighborhoods have similar geography, so it generalizes better to new areas.
885.ww: By explicitly computing water accumulation based on terrain—not just hoping the model discovers it from data—the system builds in a hint about the true physics. This forces the model to align its internal patterns with real water flow, so it can transfer what it learns in one city to another city with similar slope and drainage. The geographic learning step teaches it to treat nearby neighborhoods as similar by construction.
885.po: On a real-world urban dataset, Waterlogformer reduces prediction error compared to methods that ignore terrain or treat water collection as a pure pattern-matching puzzle. This means emergency managers can issue more accurate warnings and position trucks before streets actually flood.

886.bp: When a 911 call comes in, a human operator must stay calm, ask the right questions in sequence, and make split-second decisions about whether an ambulance or police car is needed. Training new call-takers requires them to practice hundreds of scenarios, but live role-play is expensive and constrained by how many emergencies dispatchers can realistically simulate. The goal is to let trainees practice safely and often, learning from each attempt.
886.wh: Traditional classroom role-play requires a human actor to play the caller each time, and an instructor watching to grade performance. Scaling this is slow and expensive. The obvious fix—recorded scenarios—is too rigid; every call taker branches into different questions based on what they say, so a fixed script won't work. A fully automated AI system that generates calls feels like it would just let trainees game the system by trying random words until something works.
The tension: we need AI to make the simulation responsive to each decision, but trainees need *real feedback on whether they made good choices*, not just smooth banter.
886.ap: SHIELD is a conversational AI system that generates realistic call scenarios with the AI playing the 911 caller. As a trainee responds, the system tracks exactly what they said, how long they took to respond, and what mistakes they made. After each simulated call, the AI analyzes the trainee's behavior and gives them feedback framed as a coach's insights—not just 'you were wrong,' but 'here's why that question mattered' or 'you spent 40 seconds on something that could have waited.' The feedback is designed to trigger reflection, a key principle in learning: when you think about *why* you did something, you remember the lesson.
886.ww: By logging every decision and response, the system can show trainees patterns they didn't notice themselves (e.g., they always forget to ask about allergies). By framing feedback as guidance, not judgment, trainees feel safe trying new strategies. The AI learns what good call-handling looks like from the training data, so it can spot when a trainee is heading toward a dead end and nudge them back on course.
886.po: Trainees can practice dozens of scenarios without scheduling instructors or actors, and they get personalized feedback on decision-making and timing—something a video-recorded scenario can never provide. Early testing with a real 911 center showed the system can run continuous training at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods.

887.bp: When predicting a number—like house price from its features, or crop yield from soil and weather—trees are simple and interpretable: 'if rain > 20mm, then predict high yield.' But trees rely on binary yes-or-no splits, which force them to ignore nuanced trade-offs. For example, a house might be worthwhile at a medium price *or* if it has a pool, but a binary tree struggles to capture this 'either/or' logic naturally, so it makes crude approximations and gets the prediction wrong.
887.wh: Better trees would allow multiple branches per condition, not just left-or-right, and more complex rules that capture real-world nuance. But searching through all possible multi-branch trees explodes the search space—there are far too many to try. Genetic algorithms can search huge spaces, but they often find trees with rules that sound made-up (e.g., 'if price-per-sqft > 47.2 and color is taupe, predict high'). These overfitted rules don't mean anything and fail on new houses.
The core problem: multi-branch trees are more expressive, but the search space is too vast, and existing methods produce nonsensical rules that overfit to noise.
887.ap: GraphBeam-LLM replaces trees with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)—a data structure where each decision point can branch into multiple paths, and paths can rejoin. Instead of searching randomly, the system uses beam search: at each step, it keeps only the most promising candidates and builds on those. Crucially, when generating new rules, it asks a large language model: 'what would be a sensible condition to split on here?' rather than trying random thresholds. The LLM generates conditions that sound meaningful (e.g., 'price per square foot > median for neighborhood').
887.ww: The LLM acts as a semantic filter—it steers the search toward human-understandable rules by design. Beam search ensures efficiency by focusing computational effort on promising branches rather than exploring dead ends. The graph structure itself is more powerful than trees because it allows data to flow along multiple paths and merge, capturing complex interactions between features more naturally.
887.po: On regression benchmarks (predicting abalone age, wine quality, cholesterol levels), GraphBeam-LLM reduces prediction error by 6.7% to 14.5% compared to standard tree methods. Crucially, the resulting rules are interpretable—a data scientist can explain why the model made a prediction—because the LLM ensures rules make business sense.

888.bp: Across Europe, thousands of community food-sharing projects (swap events, food banks, community gardens) operate quietly in neighborhoods, but city planners, social researchers, and community organizers have no systematic map of where they are or what they do. Building such a map would help cities understand their informal food systems and support grassroots efforts. The challenge is that these initiatives exist scattered across websites, social media, and local news—no central directory.
888.wh: Manually visiting every city's websites and social media feeds to catalog food-sharing projects is impossible; there are 200 cities and thousands of projects. Automated web scraping can find mentions of these projects, but the web is messy: you find pages in German, Italian, Polish, etc.; some are defunct, some are spam; and 'food sharing' can mean wildly different things. You can't just count the pages or infer structure from keywords alone.

The tension: we need to find these initiatives automatically across many languages and websites, but the web is a noisy, multilingual maze where genuine initiatives look similar to spam or irrelevant noise.
888.ap: The CULTIVATE system chains three automated steps. First, it translates a search query (e.g., 'community food garden') into multilingual variants using an LLM, then uses these to find candidate webpages. Second, it re-ranks and filters the results by asking the LLM to classify each page: 'Is this a genuine food-sharing initiative, or spam, or outdated?' Third, human experts manually verify the machine's classifications to catch false positives and fix errors. Then the system is scheduled to re-crawl these sites periodically to notice when projects close or new ones start. The frontend is an interactive map where users can explore these initiatives by location and type.
888.ww: By using an LLM to understand language and content semantics before classification, the system avoids brittle keyword matching. By building in human verification, it ensures quality without requiring experts to find all the initiatives manually. By re-crawling, it keeps the map current instead of becoming stale.
888.po: The SHARECITY 200 database now maps food-sharing initiatives across 200 European cities, making invisible grassroots work visible. Users can search by city and type (food bank, garden, share event, etc.), and researchers can now analyze patterns in urban food resilience. The architecture generalizes—the same pipeline works for any domain where initiatives are scattered across websites (tool libraries, repair cafes, maker spaces, etc.).

889.bp: Large language models power chatbots, code generators, and medical diagnosis assistants, but when they give an answer, how do we know if it's right? When a model predicts a medical diagnosis, we need to understand *why*—not just trust it. Explainability is the ability to tell a human what the model was thinking. Without it, we can't fix the model when it fails, and we can't trust it in high-stakes decisions.
889.wh: The traditional approach—print out which input words the model 'attended to' most—often points to irrelevant words or creates explanations that look sensible but don't reflect how the model actually works. Chain-of-Thought prompts, where the model writes out step-by-step reasoning, feel more trustworthy but are actually theater: the model is good at writing convincing narratives, not necessarily at reasoning. Recent research shows these explanations often don't match the true decision-making process, and worse, they actively mislead humans into false confidence.
The core problem: models are so complex that any single explanation is almost certainly incomplete, and the easiest explanations to generate are often lies.
889.ap: This tutorial argues for a different approach: instead of trying to fully explain *how* the model works internally—which is theoretically impossible for very large models—we should focus on what a human *needs to know* to trust or use the model effectively. This means identifying high-level concepts the model responds to (e.g., 'sentiment,' 'factuality,' 'expertise'), showing how input changes affect those concepts, and allowing humans to edit the model's behavior by modifying concepts they care about, rather than tweaking weights they don't understand.
889.ww: This approach is practical because it stops chasing an impossible ideal (perfect transparency) and instead solves the real problem: humans need to understand if the model is safe and reliable enough for their decision. By focusing on interpretable concepts, we give humans something they can actually verify and act on. By allowing inference-time intervention (e.g., 'tone down speculation'), we let humans steer the model without retraining it.
889.po: This reframes explainability from 'show the reasoning' to 'enable human-AI collaboration.' For medical diagnosis, instead of asking 'why did the model predict pneumonia?', we ask 'what symptoms is the model weighting heavily, and are those reasonable?' This is something a doctor can actually use to decide whether to trust the diagnosis.

890.bp: When a model is trained on English text, it develops a strong understanding of English concepts and relationships. If we want it to work in Mandarin or Arabic, a naive approach is to just show it examples in those languages and hope it transfers. But language models map words to numerical points in a space, and each language's word cloud is shaped differently—English clusters certain concepts together in ways that don't align with how Mandarin clusters them. So knowledge learned in English often doesn't transfer smoothly, especially when the training data in the low-resource language is small and noisy.
890.wh: When models try to share knowledge across languages, the numerical representations often collapse—all multilingual words for the same concept get squeezed together so tightly they become indistinguishable, losing nuance. At the same time, different languages encode concepts with different semantic shades, so excessive flattening destroys culturally important distinctions. The model then performs poorly on new tasks in low-resource languages, especially when the data is messy or domain-specific (different social media slang, typos, informal grammar).

Tension: multilingual models need to align concepts across languages (so 'happy' in English connects to '高兴' in Mandarin), but they also need to preserve each language's unique semantic texture and robustness to noise.
890.ap: XLingLearn adjusts how the model builds its numerical representation space. First, it computes how clustered each language's concepts are and deliberately pushes overly similar ones apart—creating more breathing room in the representation space so each semantic distinction stays sharp. Second, it adds a constraint that forces the model to learn the *same directional relationships* across languages (e.g., if 'happy' and 'sad' are opposite directions in English, the same should hold in Mandarin). Third, it stabilizes this shared direction by making sure attention patterns stay consistent across languages. Finally, it includes a debiasing term that corrects for the fact that data augmentation (adding variations of text to train) can warp the representation space in unexpected ways.
890.ww: By actively pushing representations apart rather than letting them collapse, the model preserves semantic granularity. By enforcing directional consistency, it shares *structure* across languages while allowing local differences. The debiasing term prevents augmentation tricks from introducing artifacts that hurt robustness.
890.po: When tested on cross-lingual tasks (predicting if two sentences mean the same thing, or if one entails the other), XLingLearn transfers knowledge from high-resource English to 17 low-resource languages better than prior methods. Crucially, it remains robust even when the low-resource data is noisy or when the model encounters grammatical structures it hasn't seen before—a major practical win for real-world deployments.

891.bp: When a company deploys a large language model to answer customer questions, it faces two separate problems: the model must retrieve the right information from the company's databases and documents (so it doesn't hallucinate), and it must sound like a company representative, not a generic internet chatbot. Generic models are trained on public internet text and represent world knowledge, but they don't know company policies, brand voice, or legal compliance requirements. Companies need LLMs that are both grounded in internal facts and shaped by company culture.
891.wh: Retrieval-augmented generation—looking up relevant documents and feeding them to the model—solves the hallucination problem. But the model's tone, behavior, and judgment still reflect its training on generic data. Fine-tuning the model on company examples is one option, but that's time-consuming and error-prone, and the model's core behavior doesn't change much. What's really needed is a way to layer in company-specific knowledge and style without retraining the model from scratch.
The gap: retrieval gives factual accuracy; fine-tuning gives style; but combining them robustly is hard, and the model may still make decisions that contradict company policy or brand values.
891.ap: This talk describes a hybrid approach: selective fine-tuning on high-quality examples of good company responses (so the model learns the style and judgment of experienced employees) combined with context orchestration—carefully structuring what information is retrieved and how it's presented to the model. Context orchestration means treating different types of company data differently: some facts are mandatory (legal compliance, brand values) while others are optional context (relevant documents). The system prioritizes mandatory information so the model always respects company policy, while optional context helps it sound natural.
891.ww: By fine-tuning on expert employee responses, the model learns not just facts but judgment—when to prioritize customer satisfaction versus compliance, for instance. By orchestrating context (deciding what to give the model and in what order), the system ensures critical information is never missed even if retrieval returns a weak set of documents. Together, they build an 'enterprise world model'—a system that acts like a trained employee, not a generic chatbot.
891.po: The result is an LLM that answers customer queries with accuracy (retrieval-grounded), tone (fine-tuned on internal examples), and judgment (orchestrated to prioritize policy). This talk shares the hybrid framework for building such systems at scale, treating fine-tuning and retrieval as complementary rather than competing approaches.

892.bp: Traffic forecasts are crucial for route planning, congestion warnings, and public transit scheduling. Models trained on historical traffic data can predict normal flows well, but real traffic is punctuated by accidents, weather, events, and system failures—anomalies that create sharp spikes or dips that historical patterns can't explain. A model that ignores anomalies will miss the very situations where accurate predictions matter most.
892.wh: Most deep learning traffic models optimize for average error across all conditions, which means they learn to average out anomalies rather than predict through them. When an accident causes a 30-minute jam, the model might predict a typical 5-minute delay because that's the statistical norm. Detecting and handling anomalies first seems obvious, but detecting them requires knowing what 'normal' traffic looks like, which is exactly what the forecasting model is supposed to learn. It's a chicken-and-egg problem: you need normal patterns to detect anomalies, but you need to detect anomalies to model normal patterns.
Core tension: models trained on real data (including anomalies) learn to average them out; models trained on only 'clean' data won't see real-world anomalies when deployed.
892.ap: The framework runs in two stages. Stage one: an unsupervised anomaly detector learns what normal traffic looks like by training on historical data and learning to reconstruct typical traffic flows. When the reconstruction error is high (the model struggles to explain what it sees), that's flagged as anomalous. Stage two: once anomalies are marked, a second model trained on normal patterns only will now predict the normal component of traffic flow. But to prevent the normal-patterns model from underfitting (learning only crude averages), it uses a memory module—essentially a cache of stored 'typical' traffic scenarios for each location and time—plus a sparsity constraint that encourages it to use few stored patterns per prediction, keeping explanations interpretable. The two pieces of the model (one for spatiotemporal dependencies, one for memory) work together to predict clean traffic.
892.ww: By separating anomaly detection from forecasting, the model can learn each task well. The memory module allows the model to say 'this is traffic pattern #3 that we've seen before in similar conditions,' which is more robust than trying to synthesize a prediction from scratch. The sparsity constraint prevents the model from memorizing every edge case and instead forces it to generalize.
892.po: On real traffic datasets, the model outperforms standard deep learning approaches especially during anomalous conditions—accidents, storms, events. This means navigation apps and traffic centers can issue better warnings and route recommendations when it matters most: during disruptions, not just normal flow.

893.bp: When images contain personally identifiable information—like someone's face, home address visible in a photo, or a child's name written on a shirt—people have a legal right (GDPR, COPPA) to ask platforms to remove it. But simply deleting all images with that person is extreme; the photo might also contain important scenery or other people. The goal is to remove only the specific object (a face, a license plate, a sign) while keeping the rest of the image intact and coherent.
893.wh: Traditional machine unlearning removes entire images or classes of objects. But selective removal of a single object from an image is hard: if you simply erase an object and retrain the model, the reconstruction looks wrong (a blurry hole where the object was). If you try to remove just one object's representation from a model without retraining, the model still remembers related visual features and can sometimes reconstruct it. There's no principled way to remove partial information from a model while preserving semantic coherence.

The core problem: models don't store objects as discrete, removable units; they're woven throughout the model's representations, so partial removal risks destroying the image or leaving behind recognizable traces.
893.ap: The framework uses scene graphs—structured representations of images that list objects ('person', 'car', 'tree') and their relationships ('person' is 'to the left of' 'car'). When a user requests removal of a specific object (e.g., 'remove that face'), the scene graph is edited to drop that object while keeping its relationships to other objects. The model is then retrained (or fine-tuned) using three unlearning techniques—fine-tuning on modified data, model redaction (surgically removing weights), or combinations—to 'forget' that object. The system validates that the object is actually removed (or made unrecognizable) while the rest of the image stays intact.
893.ww: By using scene graphs, unlearning becomes structured: instead of blindly erasing parts of the model, you edit the semantic description of the scene and retrain on that edited description. This ensures the model learns to generate an image without the object, rather than just deleting it or memorizing an exception. The three unlearning techniques target different layers of the model (early layers, weights, etc.), making the removal robust.
893.po: Users can request removal of specific objects ('remove that person') rather than the whole image, and the result is a realistic image with that object gone—not a blurred hole or a clearly edited artifact. This balances privacy (the object is truly gone) with utility (the rest of the image is preserved), enabling GDPR compliance without destroying valuable data.

894.bp: Machine learning companies train neural networks on massive datasets and sell access to them as services (model-as-a-service platforms). These models are valuable intellectual property, the result of expensive data and computation. But once a model is sold or deployed, the company risks losing control: competitors might reverse-engineer it, or buyers might use it in prohibited ways. Watermarking—embedding a hidden signal that proves ownership—is a practical solution, but traditional approaches require a central authority to verify ownership, which doesn't work in federated learning where many clients collaboratively train a model.
894.wh: In federated learning, the model is collectively owned and improved by many participants (hospitals, banks, etc.), each keeping their data private. If you use traditional watermarking, you need a central server to verify ownership (test the model against a secret key), but that defeats the point of federation—it reintroduces centralization. Attackers might also try to remove the watermark by fine-tuning the model on new data, or by pruning unimportant weights, or by training a smaller model that mimics the original. A centralized watermarking scheme has no way to defend against all these attacks across many clients.
Core tension: federated learning avoids central control; watermarking seems to require it. Also, watermarks need to survive multiple attacks without being noticeable to users.
894.ap: FWDV (Federated Watermarking with Distributed Verification) lets each client independently embed a watermark into its local copy of the model. Each client has its own secret key, so it can verify ownership without a central server. The framework also designs the watermark to be robust against fine-tuning, pruning, and distillation by embedding it in patterns that are hard to remove without destroying model accuracy. The watermark is hidden (it only triggers on a specific input sequence that only the owner knows), so it doesn't degrade user-facing performance.
894.ww: By distributing verification to each client, the system avoids a central bottleneck. By designing the watermark to survive pruning and fine-tuning (it's embedded in multiplicative patterns across many weights rather than isolated regions), removal becomes more costly than retraining from scratch. The hidden nature of the watermark ensures no legitimate user notices it.
894.po: On federated learning benchmarks, FWDV successfully embeds and verifies watermarks with minimal impact on model accuracy, and the watermark survives fine-tuning, pruning, and distillation attacks—making it practical for protecting collaborative models where no single party controls the system.

895.bp: City planners need to decide where to build new roads, widen existing ones, or redesign intersections to reduce congestion and improve emergency response times. The stakes are high: building a road costs millions and disrupts neighborhoods, so planners want confidence the design will actually work. Traffic simulation lets them test layouts in software before construction, but finding the optimal layout among billions of possibilities is intractable—even testing 1,000 layouts requires thousands of CPU-hours.
895.wh: Classical approaches—mathematical programming or genetic algorithms—make simplified assumptions about traffic (agents follow equations, not realistic driving behavior) to keep the search space tractable. But real traffic simulators are high-fidelity (they model realistic driver behavior, signal timing, parking, etc.), making them too slow to test many layouts. Genetic algorithms can search large spaces but often get stuck in local optima (a 'good enough' layout that isn't globally best). How do you find a genuinely excellent layout when evaluating each candidate takes minutes or hours?
Tension: realistic simulation is accurate but slow; fast search methods are crude. We need a way to search intelligently without evaluating every candidate.
895.ap: The framework uses diffusion models, a neural architecture that learns to generate new candidates by gradually adding realistic-looking details to noise. First, the system collects a dataset of randomly generated layouts and simulates each one, recording which layouts perform well (low congestion) and which perform poorly. Then, a diffusion model is trained to recognize patterns in good layouts—it learns to generate realistic, performance-aware layouts by iterating a process that gradually improves a random layout. A second neural model (a performance predictor) learns to estimate how well a given layout will perform without running the full simulation. Together, they form a search loop: generate candidates with the diffusion model, quickly rank them with the predictor, and occasionally run full simulations on the most promising ones to refine predictions.
895.ww: Diffusion models are recent neural architectures designed to generate high-quality samples; they're strong at learning the structure of good layouts from examples. The performance predictor acts as a fast proxy for simulation, allowing the search to evaluate thousands of candidates cheaply and only invest simulation time on promising ones. This dramatically reduces total computation while keeping quality high.
895.po: The system finds traffic layouts that reduce congestion and improve emergency routing—measured in the simulator—with orders of magnitude fewer simulations than brute force or genetic algorithms would require. The layouts are also more interpretable than those from pure search: because the diffusion model learns from real data, it generates layouts that obey real-world constraints without being explicitly programmed.

896.bp: Short-form video platforms (TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts) are flooded with content every second, and algorithmic recommendation systems decide what billions of people watch. Creators sometimes manipulate the algorithm by hiding text or audio in videos to trigger specific recommendations, or by stealing others' viral videos and reposting them with minor edits, hoping to capture engagement metrics. Detecting these manipulations at scale is crucial to maintain trust in the platform and fairly reward genuine creators.
896.wh: Large multimodal models (models that understand text, images, and audio together) are powerful but expensive to run on every video, and they have a tendency to hallucinate—claiming to see things that aren't there or missing subtle manipulation. A single model is also a single point of failure; if an adversary knows how one model works, they can craft videos specifically to fool it. At billions of videos per day, you can't afford to run expensive models on every candidate.

Core problem: we need to detect fine-grained manipulation (hidden text, slight color shifts, cloned audio) at massive scale, but general-purpose multimodal models are slow, prone to hallucination, and vulnerable to adversarial tricks.
896.ap: The system decomposes video understanding into three specialized roles, each optimized for one task. A Perceiver Agent examines the video in detail and extracts raw signals (text it can read, audio transcripts, objects detected, pixel-level anomalies). A Retriever Agent uses the signals to search for similar videos in a database—if the current video is highly similar to an old viral video, that's a red flag for theft. A Reviewer Agent (a high-capability reasoning model) takes the evidence from the Perceiver and Retriever and makes a final call on whether the video is original or manipulative. The system further optimizes scale by caching semantic representations of old videos (so retrieval is fast), filtering out obvious negatives early, and measuring token usage to avoid expensive computations on videos that are clearly clean.
896.ww: By decomposing the task, each agent can be optimized independently and scaled differently: the Perceiver runs on all videos, the Retriever only on suspicious ones, and the Reviewer only on difficult cases. Caching and filtering dramatically reduce compute. The appeal to retrieval ("have we seen this video before?") is powerful because content theft leaves statistical fingerprints that are hard to dodge.
896.po: The system can detect modality misalignment (hidden overlays designed to manipulate recommendations) and content theft (reposted videos) across billions of short-form videos without the compute cost or hallucination risk of running large models on everything. Creators are protected from theft, the algorithm stays honest, and the platform can scale detection.

897.bp: When recommending apps to a new user who has never used the platform before, the system has very little information—maybe just their device model or app category preferences. This is the cold-start problem: without a history of installs and ratings, generic methods (popularity rankings, category-based rules) perform poorly. New users want personalized recommendations, not just 'most popular apps.' But personalization requires understanding the user, which history provides.
897.wh: Machine learning models for recommendation combine two types of user information: static attributes (age, device type, country) and dynamic behavioral sequences (apps they've installed, time spent in each app, sequence of categories they explore). For cold-start users, behavioral data is sparse. The naive approach treats all feature types equally, but cold-start users often have strong attribute signals (clear device or location signals) that are overshadowed by missing behavior data. Models trained on both fail because they try to learn both equally, but the two feature types have different distributions and learning difficulties—attributes are stable and sparse, behaviors are sequential and rich. When attributes and behaviors are learned in the same representation, they interfere with each other.

Tension: attribute features (simple, available for new users) and behavioral sequences (rich, absent for cold-start users) have fundamentally different statistics and learning needs, so learning them together in a single model hurts cold-start performance.
897.ap: AFIM decouples learning of attributes and behavioral sequences by running them through separate pathways before combining them. Attributes flow through one lightweight module; behaviors flow through a specialized attention mechanism designed to extract user interest from sequential patterns. These separate representations are then combined in a fusion layer that decides how much to trust each source—for cold-start users, it learns to rely more on attributes because behavior data is sparse. The decoupling also includes a dynamic fusion mechanism that learns how to blend the two sources differently for different users.
897.ww: By separating the learning process, each feature type can be optimized for its own statistics and learning complexity. For cold-start users, the system naturally learns to emphasize attributes because behaviors are unavailable. The attention mechanism on behaviors ensures that rich sequential patterns (e.g., a user installing photo apps in sequence) are captured accurately, not diluted by simpler attribute signals.
897.po: On public and industrial datasets, AFIM significantly outperforms prior methods at recommending apps to cold-start users while remaining competitive for warm users. This means new users get better personalized recommendations faster, improving retention and engagement from day one.

898.bp: Large language models are exceptional at generating fluent text, but recommender systems have traditionally relied on ID-based collaborative signals—'users who liked this also liked that'—which the LLM has no access to. Recent work tries to blend the LLM's broad knowledge (understanding what a movie is about, who might enjoy it) with collaborative data (what actual users rated highly). But combining these requires being careful: merge them poorly, and the LLM's knowledge drowns out the collaborative signal, or the collaborative signal introduces noise that confuses the LLM.
898.wh: When fusing ID semantics (collaborative signals) and text semantics (LLM understanding), models face two challenges. First, fusion noise: some collaborative signals are unreliable or sparse, and naively mixing them with clean text data corrupts the recommendations. Second, semantic gap: IDs (user 1234) and text ('user who likes action movies') are fundamentally different representations, and forcing them into the same space causes friction. Simple concatenation or averaging doesn't work because the two sources have different reliability and scales.
Core tension: we want both the LLM's nuanced understanding and the collaborative data's ground truth, but they have incommensurable statistics.
898.ap: HDRec uses two separate low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules, each fine-tuning the shared LLM for one semantic source. Low-rank adaptation is a parameter-efficient method for customization: rather than retraining the entire LLM, you train a small set of parameters that reshape the LLM's behavior for your specific task. One LoRA adapts the LLM to handle collaborative ID signals; the other adapts it for text semantics. During inference (when making recommendations), the system uses text as the primary signal (it's robust) and adaptively blends in collaborative insights from the ID LoRA only if they strengthen the prediction. To prevent the two LoRAs from conflicting during training, the system alternates training between them, ensuring neither dominates.
898.ww: By using separate LoRAs, each can specialize in its own semantic source without interference. Using text as primary ensures robustness; selective blending ensures collaborative signals help when useful but don't introduce noise. Alternating training prevents the gradient conflicts that occur when two objectives pull the model in different directions.
898.po: On sequential recommendation benchmarks, HDRec outperforms both traditional collaborative filtering and pure LLM-based methods. It combines the LLM's ability to reason about item properties with the historical accuracy of collaborative signals, enabling better recommendations while remaining interpretable.

899.bp: Searching for information in one language is standard—you type a query in English and get English results. But the web is multilingual: a Spanish document about climate change may be exactly what an English speaker needs, but typical search engines return no results because the query and document are in different languages. Retrieval-augmented generation (augmenting LLM answers with retrieved documents) is becoming standard in AI systems, but if you only retrieve documents in the user's query language, you miss half the web's knowledge.
899.wh: Multilingual retrieval is hard because language-specific search algorithms—like BM25, which counts word overlaps—fail across languages. You can translate queries or documents to bridge the gap, but translation is imperfect and slow. Neural dense retrieval (mapping documents to vectors and finding similar vectors) works better, but most systems are trained on English datasets and datasets, so they're biased toward English. Extending to many languages requires training on multilingual data, which is scarce or expensive.
Tension: traditional retrieval methods (word overlap) fail across languages; neural methods need multilingual training data that's limited.
899.ap: This WSDM Cup competition challenges participants to build systems that search a multilingual document collection using English queries. The task is straightforward but reveals real challenges: retrieve relevant documents in any language, given queries in English. Participants can use translation, multilingual embeddings, or hybrid approaches, and will be evaluated on how accurately they find relevant documents regardless of language.
899.ww: By making multilingual retrieval a competition goal, the workshop surfaces practical challenges in cross-lingual search. Because the application is LLM-augmented generation (the LLM can post-process documents into the user's language), the system doesn't need to return same-language documents—it needs to return relevant ones, which LLMs can then present to the user in a readable form. This shifts the incentive from same-language matching to relevance, simplifying the problem.
899.po: Winning systems will demonstrate effective multilingual retrieval strategies that can power better search and retrieval-augmented generation in a multilingual world. The challenge surfaces state-of-the-art techniques and datasets for bridging languages in information retrieval.
